title: How do you present your structure in a case interview?
description: Interviewers weigh it heavily. Your structure is your plan for the whole case. What to do, what to say, and the mistake to avoid.
hook: Present your structure top-down: say how many areas you will look at, name each one in a sentence, say which matters most and why, and end with a hypothesis and the first piece of data you want. The structure itself should be three or four buckets tailored to this client, with no overlaps and nothing big missing. It is your plan for the whole case, so interviewers weigh it heavily.
body:
Stage 4 of 10 in the ten stages of a case.

Why the structure matters

Your structure is your plan for the rest of the case. A good one tells you what data to ask for, in what order, and makes the final recommendation easy to assemble. A weak one leaves you wandering. It is the stage candidates practise most and still the one that goes wrong most often, usually for the same two reasons: generic buckets that would fit any company, and no hypothesis.

Build it in three checks

1. Three or four buckets, tailored to this client

Draw three or four first-level buckets. Under each, write two or three short drivers that are specific to this client and this problem. "Revenue, costs, market" is a start. "In-store vs delivery volume, average ticket by channel, app commissions" is a structure for a coffee chain whose profit fell after it joined delivery apps.

Use factors for "why" questions (why has profit fallen?) and criteria for "should we" questions (should we enter this market?). More on choosing a shape in how to structure your answer.

2. Check it is MECE

Before you speak, check that the buckets do not overlap and that nothing big is missing, such as regulation, competition or an industry-wide shift. Overlaps make you count the same thing twice. Gaps mean you can miss the answer entirely. See what MECE means and how to build it.

3. Make sure it can produce an answer

The best structures can be measured. Suppose a bank's customer complaints have risen. Buckets called "customers, company, competition" are broad but hard to test. A sharper version starts with an equation:

Complaints = transactions × complaints per transaction

Then split the complaint rate by customer journey: onboarding, payments, lending and support. Within the worst journey, look at specific failure points. Now every branch tells you what data to request.

Here is why the equation helps. Say the bank handled 40M transactions last year at a complaint rate of 0.10%, which is 40,000 complaints. This year it handled 50M at 0.12%, which is 60,000. At last year's rate, 50M transactions would have produced 50,000 complaints, so growth in volume explains 10,000 of the extra complaints and a worse complaint rate explains the other 10,000. Half of the rise is the bank simply getting bigger. Your structure revealed that before you looked at a single journey.

Present it top-down

Lead with the big points, number them and end with where you would start:

  1. Signpost: "There are three areas I'd like to look at."
  2. Name each bucket in one sentence, with one or two drivers. Do not read out every leaf.
  3. Prioritise: "I think the second is most likely the issue, because..."
  4. Ask for data: "So I'd like to start there. Do we have...?"

Turn your page so the interviewer can see it. On a video call, hold it up or describe it clearly; Bain's guidance for virtual interviews asks candidates to clearly describe their structure.

Weak and strong

A market entry case: should a coffee chain enter a new country?

Weak: "I'd look at the market, the competition, the company and the financials. Where would you like me to start?"
Strong: "There are three areas I want to look at. First, whether the market is attractive: its size, growth and margins. Second, whether we can win against the local chains already there. Third, whether the economics work: investment, payback and risks. I believe the second is the deciding factor because the market is crowded, so I'd start there. Do we have data on the main competitors' share?"

The strong version is numbered, tailored, prioritised and ends with a request. The weak one hands the case back to the interviewer.

Common mistakes

  • A memorised framework with the client's name on top. Interviewers recognise it instantly. Tailor the drivers.
  • Too many buckets. Seven buckets is a list, not a structure. Group them.
  • Reading out every leaf. Give the headline of each bucket and one or two drivers.
  • No hypothesis. Say which bucket matters most and why, even if you might be wrong.
  • Never coming back to it. Tick off branches as you go, and use the structure to choose your next step.

Practise the moment

Say your answer out loud before you open the model.

1. You have finished presenting your structure. What do you not say?

Show a strong answer

Not: "Where would you like me to start?" Instead: "I believe X is most likely the issue, because... Do we have data on that?"

Why it works: A hypothesis shows you are solving the problem, not just organising it.

2. A hotel's revenue has fallen 10%. Give a measurable first level for your structure.

Show a strong answer

"Revenue is rooms available × occupancy × average room rate, plus non-room revenue such as food and events. I'd first check which of those moved, then split the one that did by customer segment, such as business and leisure."

Why it works: Each branch can be checked with one number, so the first data request is obvious.

3. You have drawn six first-level buckets for a cost case. What do you do?

Show a strong answer

Group them into three or four. For example, put "raw materials", "packaging" and "freight" under "variable costs", and "rent" and "salaries" under "fixed costs". Then add one more if something big, such as one-off costs, is missing.

Why it works: Fewer, larger buckets are easier to present, easier to follow and easier to prioritise.

Where to practise next

Structuring improves with volume. Use the structuring drill for quick reps, then work through a practice set such as 17 profitability structuring questions. For the next stage, read how to lead the case by proposing the next step.
